doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Radio, records and radio wires at Birdland and the Hickory House
summary: Early musicians feared recording; radio remotes built bands and made clubs like Birdland known nationally.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: The radio was a really big part of spreading this music.

Oh, yeah. And radio, I mean there weren’t the number of people producing stuff for radio. And advertisers didn’t understand how valuable radio was. Musicians didn’t understand how valuable the advertising of having a record was. There were early musicians that wouldn’t record because they were afraid that people would steal their music. So the first people who recorded became insanely popular.
Wasn’t that the story with Freddie Keppard? And he passed up the chance to be the first Dixieland group?

Yeah. Wouldn’t record. But as soon as people began to realize that then to get a record was important if you wanted to be a popular band, and to get a job in a club that had a radio wire at night was important. That was one of the big things that built the bands at the Hickory House. I used to work there with Marian McPartland. But in the years before that, when they were first starting out, at night, they didn’t have a whole lot of sponsored programs. So all the radio stations would put telephone wires into the local nightclubs and ballrooms, and they would send a guy out to do a half hour remote. Birdland became very nationally known just because they had a radio wire. And every Tuesday night when the new act would come in, the first set was broadcast on the radio. Everybody turned on, say, “Hey that sounds good,” they’d go down and hear the music. But not only that, people out of town would get these programs. And when they came to New York they had an address that they knew and a place to go, you know. It made all the difference in the world. It was wonderful. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
